MARKUP-ANALYSIS MEMORANDUM
CFIUS National Security Agreement — Counterparty Redline Review

TO:      Deal Team / Client
FROM:    International Trade & Sanctions Counsel
DATE:    [Engagement Date]
RE:      Risk-Prioritized Analysis of Counterparty Markup to Draft CFIUS National Security Agreement (NSA); Recommendations and Counter-Draft Language
FILE:    international-trade-sanctions — Analyze Counterparty Markup of CFIUS National Security Agreement
OUTPUT:  markup-analysis-memo.docx

================================================================================
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY AND RISK PRIORITIZATION
================================================================================

We reviewed the counterparty's markup of the draft CFIUS National Security Agreement against (i) the firm base draft NSA and supporting deal materials, (ii) Disclosure Schedules 3.7 and 5.2 and Exhibit B (survival matrix), and (iii) the controlling deal-team instruction in the latest partner correspondence. Misfiled correspondence from unrelated engagements in the matter folder was disregarded.

The counterparty accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations. Reconciled against the schedules and the controlling client instruction, we prioritize as follows:

  PRIORITY 1 — WALK-AWAY / CRITICAL
  Shortened survival / limitation period for core representations (contradicts Exhibit B; client treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue).

  PRIORITY 2 — HIGH / MUST PUSH BACK HARD
  Material Adverse Effect (MAE) definition expanded with carve-outs for regulatory action of the type at issue (intersects Schedule 3.7 pending regulatory inquiries; would hollow out the MAE walk-right and related conditions in a CFIUS/sanctions-sensitive deal).

  PRIORITY 3 — MEDIUM / NEGOTIABLE PER CLIENT INSTRUCTION
  Indemnification: silent reduction of the indemnification cap, and conversion of the basket from deductible to tipping basket. Client will concede the basket conversion. The silent cap reduction remains objectionable and must be restored or expressly renegotiated; Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities amplify the economic shift if the cap is left reduced.

Overall recommendation: Reject the survival-period change without compromise consistent with Exhibit B; reject the MAE regulatory carve-outs (or narrowly cabin them so they cannot swallow Schedule 3.7 risk); concede tipping-basket mechanics only; restore the indemnification cap to the base draft amount and make any cap change bilateral, visible, and priced.

================================================================================
II. SCOPE, BASELINE, AND RECONCILIATION METHOD
================================================================================

A. Baseline Documents
  1. Draft CFIUS National Security Agreement (firm form / base materials) — representations and warranties, covenants, conditions to closing, indemnification, termination, and related defined terms.
  2. Counterparty markup (deviations identified below).
  3. Schedule 3.7 — discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect the markup's MAE carve-outs.
  4. Schedule 5.2 — lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift.
  5. Exhibit B — sets the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts; scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.
  6. Controlling deal correspondence — latest partner message: client will concede basket conversion; any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue. Earlier contrary priority ordering in the thread is superseded and was not followed.

B. Method
For each deviation we (1) state the base position, (2) state the counterparty change, (3) reconcile against schedules/exhibits, (4) assess CFIUS / international-trade-sanctions and commercial risk, (5) map to client instruction, (6) recommend Accept / Reject / Counter, and (7) supply counter-draft language suitable for insertion into the next turn of the NSA.

C. Practice Context
This is a CFIUS National Security Agreement in an international trade sanctions matter. MAE, survival, and indemnification allocations interact directly with pending regulatory inquiries, mitigation obligations to CFIUS/Treasury, sanctions compliance, and post-closing government engagement. Carve-outs and shortened survival that are merely "market" in ordinary M&A are often unacceptable where the core deal risk is regulatory.

================================================================================
III. PRIORITY 1 — SURVIVAL / LIMITATION PERIOD FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS
================================================================================

A. Base Position
Under the base draft NSA and Exhibit B (survival matrix), core representations — including those addressing CFIUS, national security commitments, ownership and control, sanctions/export controls, government contracts touching covered assets, and fundamental corporate authority — survive for the periods specified in Exhibit B (typically longer-dated or, for specified fundamental/regulatory reps, through the applicable statute of limitations or a multi-year post-closing period). Exhibit B controls over general survival language.

B. Counterparty Markup
The markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations, compressing the window in which Buyer (or the protected party) may bring indemnification or other contractual claims for breach of those reps.

C. Reconciliation to Schedules / Exhibits
  • Exhibit B sets the operative survival matrix. The markup's shortened limitation period directly contradicts Exhibit B.
  • Scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials. Any markup that silently overrides Exhibit B without amending Exhibit B is ineffective as a matter of document hierarchy and must be rejected or forced into an express Exhibit B amendment that the client has already indicated it will not accept if it reduces survival.
  • Schedule 3.7's pending regulatory inquiries may not fully crystallize into claims, orders, or losses until after a shortened survival period would have expired — making shortened survival especially damaging in this fact pattern.

D. Risk Assessment (CRITICAL / WALK-AWAY)
  • Client instruction (controlling): any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue.
  • Substantive risk: Core CFIUS/sanctions reps are precisely the reps most likely to be tested by post-signing or post-closing government action, mitigation non-compliance allegations, or discovery of undisclosed foreign nexus. A shortened period shifts latent regulatory risk entirely to the protected party.
  • Process risk: A "silent" or general limitation-period insert that is not mapped to Exhibit B creates ambiguity and litigation risk over which instrument controls.
  • Recommendation: REJECT in full. Do not trade survival reduction for basket or other economics. Restore Exhibit B matrix expressly.

E. Disposition
REJECT — walk-away if counterparty insists on any reduction of survival for core/fundamental/regulatory representations relative to Exhibit B.

F. Counter-Draft Language

  Option 1 — Restore and elevate Exhibit B (preferred):

    "Section [X] Survival. The representations, warranties, covenants, and agreements contained in this Agreement shall survive the Closing for the periods set forth in Exhibit B (Survival Matrix), which Exhibit B is incorporated by reference and shall control over any conflicting general limitation period in this Agreement or any ancillary document. No amendment, waiver, or side letter shall shorten the survival periods applicable to the Fundamental Representations, the CFIUS/National Security Representations, or the Sanctions and Export Control Representations without the prior written consent of [Buyer/Protected Party], and any purported shortening without such consent shall be void. Claims asserted in writing in reasonable detail before the applicable survival expiration date shall survive until finally resolved."

  Option 2 — Explicit non-derogation:

    "Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement (including any general contractual limitation period), the survival periods in Exhibit B shall not be reduced, and the parties agree that Exhibit B as attached to the base draft dated [date] remains unmodified."

  Negotiation note: If counterparty seeks only a clarification (not a reduction), accept a clean cross-reference to Exhibit B without changing any duration.

================================================================================
IV. PRIORITY 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT DEFINITION — REGULATORY CARVE-OUTS
================================================================================

A. Base Position
The base draft MAE definition is the firm-standard formulation for a CFIUS-sensitive transaction: a Material Adverse Effect means a material adverse effect on the business, assets, results, or condition of the covered business, or on the ability of the relevant party to consummate the transaction and perform the NSA mitigation obligations, subject only to limited customary carve-outs (e.g., general economic, industry-wide, or market changes, to the extent not disproportionately affecting the company). Regulatory actions of the type central to this matter — CFIUS review/mitigation, sanctions designations or enforcement, export-control actions, and analogous national-security measures — are not carved out of MAE in the base draft, precisely because they are deal-critical risks.

B. Counterparty Markup
The definition of Material Adverse Effect adds carve-outs for regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter (CFIUS/national security, sanctions, and related regulatory measures). As drafted by counterparty, such actions would not constitute, and would be excluded from, an MAE.

C. Reconciliation to Schedules / Exhibits
  • Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect these carve-outs. If MAE excludes "regulatory action" of this type, then adverse developments in, or arising from, the Schedule 3.7 inquiries — including expansion of scope, interim orders, mitigation escalation, or enforcement — could not support an MAE-based closing condition failure, termination right, or related remedy, even if they destroy the value or feasibility of the deal.
  • The scheduled disclosure qualifies the representation; it does not, and should not, eliminate MAE protection for post-disclosure deterioration or for effects outside the four corners of the scheduled description.
  • Combined with Priority 1 (shortened survival), the MAE carve-out would leave the protected party with neither a pre-closing walk right nor a meaningful post-closing claim period for the central risk of the transaction.

D. Risk Assessment (HIGH)
  • In a CFIUS NSA, the principal non-ordinary-course risk is regulatory. Carving that risk out of MAE inverts the purpose of the definition in this deal type.
  • Schedule 3.7 makes the issue concrete, not hypothetical: two pending inquiries are already on the record. Counterparty's carve-out would convert disclosed risk into unremedied residual risk borne by our client.
  • Downstream effects: conditions to closing keyed to no-MAE; bring-down of reps; termination fee / reverse termination fee triggers; and financing conditions may all be impaired.
  • Recommendation: REJECT broad regulatory carve-outs. If any regulatory carve-out is discussed, limit it to generally applicable changes in law that do not disproportionately affect the company and that expressly exclude CFIUS mitigation, the Schedule 3.7 matters, sanctions enforcement against the company or its beneficial owners, and any order impairing NSA performance.

E. Disposition
REJECT the counterparty MAE regulatory carve-outs as written. COUNTER with a narrow, disproportionate-effect formulation that preserves MAE coverage for Schedule 3.7 matters and CFIUS/sanctions actions specific to the company or the transaction.

F. Counter-Draft Language

  "Material Adverse Effect" means any change, event, effect, state of facts, or occurrence that has had, or would reasonably be expected to have, a material adverse effect on (i) the business, assets, liabilities, properties, financial condition, or results of operations of the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, or (ii) the ability of [Seller/Company] to consummate the transactions contemplated by this Agreement or to perform its obligations under this Agreement or any CFIUS mitigation commitment, National Security Agreement, or related letter of assurance;

  provided, however, that none of the following shall be deemed, either alone or in combination, to constitute a Material Adverse Effect, or be taken into account in determining whether a Material Adverse Effect has occurred or would reasonably be expected to occur:

    (a) changes in general economic, political, or market conditions;
    (b) changes generally affecting the industry in which the Company operates;
    (c) changes in applicable generally applicable Law or GAAP after the date hereof;

  except, in the case of clauses (a)–(c), to the extent such change, event, effect, state of facts, or occurrence has a disproportionate adverse effect on the Company and its Subsidiaries, taken as a whole, relative to other participants in the same industry;

  and provided, further, that in no event shall any of the following be excluded from Material Adverse Effect or from the determination thereof:

    (1) any action, investigation, inquiry, order, directive, or mitigation requirement by CFIUS, the U.S. Department of the Treasury, or any other U.S. national security, sanctions, or export-control authority relating to the Company, its equityholders, the Covered Assets, or the transactions contemplated hereby (including any development with respect to the matters disclosed on Schedule 3.7);
    (2) any sanctions designation, enforcement action, or export-control restriction applicable to the Company, its Subsidiaries, or their respective directors, officers, or beneficial owners; or
    (3) any material breach of, or inability to perform, obligations under this National Security Agreement or any related mitigation agreement.

  Negotiation fallback (only if needed to close a narrow gap): permit exclusion of "generally applicable changes in sanctions or export-control regulations that do not target the Company or the industry segment of the Company and do not disproportionately affect the Company," while retaining full inclusion of Schedule 3.7 developments and company-specific CFIUS action.

================================================================================
V. PRIORITY 3 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION
================================================================================

A. Base Position
Base draft NSA / purchase-agreement indemnity architecture (as applicable to breaches of NSA-related and transaction reps/covenants):
  • Indemnification cap at the firm-standard negotiated ceiling (purchase-price percentage or fixed dollar cap in the base draft).
  • Basket structured as a true deductible (losses recovered only above the basket; basket amount not recoverable).
  • Fundamental / CFIUS / sanctions / fraud claims typically uncapped or subject to a higher separate cap, and often with no basket or a separate lower basket.

B. Counterparty Markup
  1. The indemnification cap is silently reduced (amount lowered without conspicuous call-out or reciprocal concession).
  2. The basket is converted from a deductible to a tipping (first-dollar, threshold) basket — once the threshold is reached, losses are recoverable from dollar one.

C. Reconciliation to Schedules / Exhibits
  • Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities. A reduced cap, combined with those retained liabilities, silently shifts economic exposure: liabilities that were expected to sit with Seller (or the indemnifying party) up to the original cap may now exceed the reduced cap and fall on Buyer (or the protected party).
  • The "silent" character of the cap change is itself a process defect — material economic terms should be redlined transparently and tied to the consideration / price adjustment discussion.
  • Basket conversion interacts with Schedule 5.2: a tipping basket is more buyer-friendly once the threshold is met; a reduced cap is more seller-friendly. Net economics depend on expected loss distribution. Client instruction addresses only the basket.

D. Risk Assessment and Client Instruction
  • Controlling client instruction: the client will concede the basket conversion (deductible → tipping). Reflect that concession in the next draft.
  • Cap reduction: NOT covered by the concession. Silent reduction is unacceptable. Restore base-draft cap. If counterparty seeks a lower cap, require express negotiation, visibility in the redline, and either price adjustment or expansion of carve-outs from the cap (fundamental reps, CFIUS/sanctions, Schedule 5.2 items, fraud).
  • Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities must remain recoverable and should be carved out of the general cap or subject to the higher fundamental cap.
  • Recommendation: ACCEPT tipping basket; REJECT silent cap reduction; COUNTER to restore cap and harden Schedule 5.2 / regulatory carve-outs from the cap.

E. Disposition
  • Basket (deductible → tipping): ACCEPT per controlling client instruction.
  • Indemnification cap reduction: REJECT; restore base amount; require any future cap discussion to be express and consideration-linked.
  • Schedule 5.2 / fundamental / CFIUS claims: confirm uncapped or higher-capped treatment and no basket (or separate basket) as in base draft.

F. Counter-Draft Language

  1. Basket (ACCEPT — tipping / threshold form):

    "Basket. The Indemnifying Party shall not be liable for indemnification under Section [Rep Breach Indemnity] unless and until the aggregate amount of all Losses subject to indemnification thereunder exceeds $[Basket Amount] (the "Basket"), in which event the Indemnifying Party shall be liable for all such Losses from the first dollar (including Losses comprising the Basket). The Basket shall not apply to Losses arising out of or relating to (i) fraud, willful misconduct, or intentional misrepresentation, (ii) breaches of Fundamental Representations, (iii) breaches of CFIUS, National Security, Sanctions, or Export Control Representations or covenants, or (iv) the retained liabilities set forth on Schedule 5.2."

  2. Cap (REJECT reduction — restore base):

    "Cap. Except with respect to claims for fraud, willful misconduct, intentional misrepresentation, breaches of Fundamental Representations, breaches of CFIUS/National Security/Sanctions/Export Control Representations or covenants, and the retained liabilities set forth on Schedule 5.2 (as to which there shall be no cap / a cap equal to the Purchase Price), the aggregate liability of the Indemnifying Party under Section [Rep Breach Indemnity] shall not exceed $[Base Draft Cap Amount] (the "Cap"). For the avoidance of doubt, the Cap remains as set forth in the base draft of this Agreement dated [base draft date] and has not been reduced."

  3. Anti-silence / transparency rider (optional process protection):

    "No amendment to the Cap, the Basket, or the categories of Losses excluded from the Cap or Basket shall be effective unless set forth in a written instrument that expressly identifies the prior amount or standard and the new amount or standard."

  4. Schedule 5.2 protection:

    "Schedule 5.2 Retained Liabilities. Notwithstanding the Cap or the Basket, the Indemnifying Party shall indemnify the Indemnified Party for all Losses arising out of or relating to the matters set forth on Schedule 5.2, without regard to the Cap or the Basket, and nothing in the counterparty markup shall be construed to shift Schedule 5.2 liabilities to the Indemnified Party."

================================================================================
VI. CROSS-ISSUE INTERACTIONS AND PACKAGE POSITION
================================================================================

The three deviations are more dangerous in combination than alone:

  1. MAE regulatory carve-outs + Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries → weak pre-closing exit if regulatory situation deteriorates.
  2. Shortened survival contradicting Exhibit B → weak post-closing recovery if the same regulatory risks mature into losses after closing.
  3. Reduced indemnification cap + Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities → even timely claims may be economically truncated.

Together, these would reallocate the core CFIUS/sanctions risk of the deal onto our client while preserving counterparty deal certainty. That package is inconsistent with the purpose of a National Security Agreement mitigation framework and with the controlling client instruction on survival.

Package negotiation posture:
  • Non-negotiable: Exhibit B survival matrix (no reduction); MAE coverage for company-specific CFIUS/sanctions/Schedule 3.7 matters; restoration of indemnification cap; Schedule 5.2 carved out of cap/basket.
  • Conceded: tipping basket mechanics (per latest partner instruction).
  • Tradeable only with express client approval: minor MAE drafting cleanup that does not expand regulatory carve-outs; cosmetic indemnity process terms (claim notice mechanics, sole-remedy clauses) that do not cut quantum or duration.

================================================================================
VII. ISSUE-BY-ISSUE RECOMMENDATION TABLE
================================================================================

| # | Deviation                         | Base / Controlling Source      | Risk     | Client Instruction      | Disposition              |
|---|-----------------------------------|--------------------------------|----------|-------------------------|--------------------------|
| 1 | Shortened survival / limitation for core reps | Exhibit B survival matrix     | Critical | Walk-away if reduced    | REJECT; restore Exhibit B |
| 2 | MAE carve-outs for regulatory action of the type at issue | Base MAE; Schedule 3.7        | High     | Protect regulatory risk | REJECT broad carve-out; COUNTER narrow language |
| 3a| Basket: deductible → tipping      | Base deductible basket         | Medium   | Concede conversion      | ACCEPT tipping basket    |
| 3b| Silent reduction of indemnity cap | Base cap; Schedule 5.2         | Medium-High | Not conceded          | REJECT; restore base cap; protect Schedule 5.2 |

================================================================================
VIII. RECOMMENDED NEXT STEPS
================================================================================

1. Circulate this memorandum and obtain client confirmation that Priority 1 remains walk-away and that basket conversion remains conceded.
2. Send counterparty a responsive redline implementing:
   • Exhibit B survival restored and controlling (Section III.F);
   • MAE definition per Section IV.F (no regulatory carve-out for CFIUS/sanctions/Schedule 3.7);
   • Tipping basket accepted; base cap restored; Schedule 5.2 and fundamental/CFIUS claims excluded from cap and basket (Section V.F).
3. Require counterparty to confirm in writing that no other "silent" economic changes appear in definitions, schedules, or annexes.
4. Align conditions to closing, bring-down, and termination provisions with the final MAE definition so no orphaned cross-references remain.
5. Update the disclosure schedules only as needed to keep Schedule 3.7 and Schedule 5.2 descriptions current; do not expand MAE carve-outs via schedule drafting.
6. Escalate immediately if counterparty re-inserts survival reductions or broad regulatory MAE carve-outs.

================================================================================
IX. CONCLUSION
================================================================================

Every identified deviation in the counterparty markup has been reconciled against the base CFIUS NSA materials, Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, Exhibit B, and the controlling (latest) deal-team instruction. We recommend a firm reject-and-counter on survival and MAE regulatory carve-outs, acceptance limited to the tipping-basket conversion, and full restoration of the indemnification cap with express protection for Schedule 5.2 and CFIUS/sanctions/fundamental claims. Counter-draft language for each material change is set forth above for insertion into the next NSA turn.

END OF MEMORANDUM
